      CARPENTER LAND AND CATTLE CO.’S LIMITED EXCEPTIONS TO THE
      ALTERNATIVE RECOMMENDATION IN THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

        Carpenter Land and Cattle Co. (Carpenter) files these Limited Exceptions (Exceptions) to

 the alternative recommendation of route selection offered in the Proposal for Decision (PFD).

 Pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies Memorandum, filed August 20, 2026, these Limited

 Exceptions are timely filed on or before September 2, 2026. Carpenter does not except to the

 primary recommendation in the Proposal for Decision.

                                       I.     INTRODUCTION

        The Carpenter family raises these limited exceptions focused solely on       the PFD’s

 alternative routing recommendation of Route 894. The Carpenters have owned Greenwood

 Creek Ranch on the east side of the Colorado River for generations.1 This is the point at which

 Route 894 would cross the Colorado River just south of the Colorado Bend State Park and the

 recently acquired Post Oak Ridge State Park.2 The Carpenter family excepts to this routing

 recommendation because it will have permanent and scarring impacts on the Colorado River and
        1
            Carpenter Ex. 1, Carpenter Dir. at 6.
        2
            Id. at 9.
                                                                                                      Page 3 of 18


its tributary Greenwood Creek.3 It would be permanently devastating to Greenwood Creek

Ranch and the adjacent State Parks and would run at cross-purposes with all of the traditions of

the Carpenter family to preserve and protect the special place in Texas.4

       If the Commission selects a route in this proceeding at this time, Carpenter urges the

Commission to select a route that limits the crossing of the Colorado River to a previously

disturbed corridor. In particular, the record supports selection of Route 296, which crosses the

Colorado River in an area that is already disturbed and is crossed by multiple large pipelines.5

       The PFD’s routing analysis does not appear to properly weigh the import of the impact to

this area of the Colorado River and ignores relevant Commission precedent that supports

rejection of Route 894, in particular where it would cross the Colorado River in proximity to the

Colorado Bend State Park and the recently acquired Post Oak Ridge State Park.6 Accordingly, if

the Commission overturns the primary recommendation in the PFD on need, Carpenter urges the

Commission to review all available routing options and conduct a robust analysis of the record

evidence and Commission precedent. Such an analysis will support selection of Route 296,

which better addresses the routing factors required by applicable law.

                                    II.     APPLICABLE LAW

       The PFD recommends the selection of the Applicants’ “best meets” Route 894; however,

this single issue route on which Route 894 best meets the applicable criteria is focused solely on

a counting of habitable structures within the notice corridor established by Commission rule.

This myopic focus does not                represent a proper consideration of the statutory factors,

Commission rules, or Commission precedent; it ignores the well-developed record that this route

       3

is contrary to community values, disproportionately impacts the use of two major Texas State

Parks, bisects historic long-held multigenerational properties along the Colorado River, has

unaddressed serious environmental impacts, and treats a select few structures as constraints that

through minor modifications could be avoided. No single routing factor is dispositive, and the

Carpenter family urges that the Commission consider all of the routing factors proportionally.

                                    III.    EXCEPTIONS

       Carpenter respectfully submits these Exceptions, which are limited to the PFD’s

alternative routing recommendation of Route 894. Carpenter focuses these exceptions on what

they know best-- the area of Route 894 on Greenwood Creek Ranch that crosses the Colorado

River at an undisturbed point.7 There are many other reasons that Route 894 is not the best route

when considering all appropriate factors.               To avoid redundancy, these exceptions will not

address each and every factor and Carpenter respectfully requests the Commission carefully

consider the entirety of the record and all of those arguments raised by other parties that refute

the proposed recommendation of Route 894.


       A. Routing Criteria
                 i. Community Values

       The PFD does not properly consider the community value impacts of selection of Route

894 which would cross the Colorado River on Carpenter’s Greenwood Creek Ranch.8 The J22

crossing of the Colorado River sits within the Greenwood Ranch and is in the viewshed of both

Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.9 These parks are deeply valued by the

           Id.

affected community and the Carpenters,10 and the negative impacts of Link J22 on community

values, should be weighed more thoroughly by the Commission.11

       The protection of the Colorado River is an essential feature in the study area that is

valued by the communities in the area and statewide.12 All proposed routes cross the Colorado

River. The point at which that crossing occurs will impact the affected community. The PFD

does not contend that the crossing of the Colorado River using Link J22 in Route 894 is the least

harmful on the community.

       In Finding of Fact No. 175, the PFD states that community values considered a wide

variety of concerns. The PFD even highlights landowner concerns related to community values,

outright acknowledging that “[t]he Carpenter Family has preserved and protected the natural

beauty of the Colorado River for almost 100 years to the benefit of the community....”13

However, the PFD cannot overstate the far reaching and irreparable impacts to Greenwood Creek

Ranch that would result from construction of Route 894.14 Even with the well-developed record

on the detriment Route 894 brings to community values, the PFD still recommends Route 894

supported only by Finding of Fact No. 176, that “Route 894 adequately addresses the expressed

community values.” The Colorado River and the affected community should be fully considered

and not be relegated to an “adequate” approach.

       The PFD focuses significant discussions of community impacts on Florence Elementary

School on Link F34. As discussed below, the potential impact on this structure can be mitigated

without the bounds of this case and should not serve to eliminate routing options that avoid

running contrary to Commission precedent by materially impacting the community’s enjoyment

of the Colorado River at Greenwood Creek Ranch nor should it result in selection of a route that

impairs the public use of the Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks.

       Choosing Route 894 based on one structure and alleged prudent avoidance is not a

subjective balancing of routing factors as required under the statute and the Commission’s rules.

                       ii. Recreation and Park Areas

       Carpenter also excepts to Findings of Fact 193-195 and Conclusion of Law 16 to the

extent that it supports Route 894. The PFD’s recommended route fails to appropriately consider

impacts to Texas State Parks. The record shows that if Route 894 were selected, the line would

be seen from both Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park,15 using the historic

and preserved Carpenter property as its vessel, specifically crossing along the highest point on

the property.16

       Because viewshed is a priority for TPWD, it recommended setting the selected route

farther from the boundary of Post Oak Ridge State Park to protect the viewshed of the

headquarters, trailhead, and Post Oak Falls overlook, and the Colorado Bend State Park.19

       The PFD undervalues this recommendation and, as a result, selected a route among the

worst possible options for crossing the Colorado River when considering the southern facing

views from the Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.            In addition to

viewshed obstruction, Link J22 (and J26) introduce disturbance corridors into the Colorado

River environment while also in close proximity to highly valued recreational resources.20

Further, the evidence shows that Link J22 would come between locations of park ranger facilities

that are within the Vann Ranch, which shares a property line with Greenwood Creek Ranch.21

        Accordingly, the impacts to recreation and parks argue strongly against selecting Route

894. This is coupled with the fact that a preexisting disturbed area that coincides with compatible

ROW and existing infrastructure, while also sitting farther from the state parks, can be used in

this case by selecting Route 296.22 These impacts cannot and should not be dismissed by using

a distance metric that is not indicative of the actual park impacts.

                          iii. Historic Values

        Carpenter also excepts to Findings of Fact 198-201 and Conclusion of Law 16 to the

extent that it supports Route 894. The Carpenter family has preserved and protected Greenwood

Creek Ranch for many generations.23 Greenwood Creek Ranch has historically served the

community through extensive gatherings focused on the use and enjoyment of the natural beauty

the family has preserved.24 This Ranch protects a significant portion of the east bank of the

Colorado River just south of what is now Post Oak Ridge State Park and has preserved the

natural beauty of the Colorado River for over 100 years for the benefit of its community and

neighbors.25 The history of the Ranch is included in record evidence through the testimony of

John Carpenter.26 As detailed in extensive pictures and personal accounts, Greenwood Creek

Ranch is surrounded by springs and pools and a mountaintop lookout.27

       Link J22 goes directly over the highest point of the Ranch at the lookout and would

forever change the views at the Ranch.28 It also bisects the ranch as it turns near the banks of the

Colorado River, coming between the two riverfront structures - Greenwood Creek Ranch Lodge

which has historically been used extensively to host gatherings of family and visitors and the

guest house to the north.29

       When the routing factors are considered as a whole and with the acknowledgment

that historic ranches and sites are also present on Link J22 and G51-G52, it is clear that

Route 296 is superior to Route 894.

                          iv. Environmental Integrity

       Carpenter excepts to Findings of Fact 205-213 and 222-223 and Conclusion of Law 16,

because the evidence does not support these findings.                         The Carpenter Family, through

Greenwood Creek Ranch, has preserved and protected the natural beauty of the Colorado River

for nearly a century, and is one of the longest continuously occupied homes on its banks in the

area.30 The PFD fails to acknowledge the specific evidence on the environmental impacts on the

Colorado River, its contributing springs, and Greenwood Creek—all of which will negatively

affect Greenwood Creek Ranch.

       The Carpenter family sponsored expert testimony documenting the devastating impacts

the waters of the US, including the Colorado River, on Greenwood Creek Ranch.31 Greenwood

Creek runs in an east to west direction on the northern portion of Greenwood Creek Ranch.32 As

such, Link J22 has detrimental impacts to all aspects of the creek which would in turn have

detrimental impacts on the Colorado River.33 These documented environmental integrity of the

region that would be associated with Route 894 are not addressed in the PFD.

       On the issue of river crossings, the PFD refers only to arguments supporting crossing the

Colorado River via Routes 296 and 392, and it ultimately concludes that using existing corridors

is the environmentally superior option.34 It does nothing to explain why it is suitable to cross the

Colorado River via Route 894, especially considering the extent to which the record developed

issues with habitat disturbance/fragmentation and visual impacts to State Parks.35 As endorsed

and discussed above, it is best to co-locate new infrastructure parallel to or in close proximity to

existing corridors, rather than in native areas.36 Using a pipeline corridor, as available in 296,

consolidates environmental disturbance and reduces fragmentation in a particularly scenic area.37

       An additional and unique environmental concern with the J22 crossing is that, unlike

Routes 296 and 572, it requires a turning structure on Greenwood Creek Ranch within close

proximity to the river.38 A turning structure will require deeper excavation and concrete footings

than a new 765kV standard (or tangent) structure. Not only are the standard footing structures of

great concern from a groundwater intrusion perspective across the study area, but J22 and J26

also present significant concern for structural integrity, throughflow and drainage, and potential

for increased erosion to the Colorado River and the many nearby creeks and potential wetlands.39

While the PFD recognizes concerns about habitat fragmentation and State Park visibility

associated with Route 894, it fails to recognize that this additional concern unique to Route 894.

       Route 296 reduces the detrimental environmental impacts to the Colorado River, state

parks, and Greenwood Creek ranch by avoiding crossing at Link J22.40 Accordingly, Carpenter

excepts to the Findings of Fact 205-213 and 222-223 and Conclusion of Law 16 to the extent that

they support 894 and asks the Commission to select a route that avoids crossing the Colorado

River at J22. This can be accomplished by selecting Route 296.

                     v. Cost

       Carpenter also excepts to Findings of Fact 224-227 and Conclusion of Law 16 to the

extent that it supports Route 894. The PFD’s ultimate routing recommendation indicates that it

did not find cost to be a distinguishing factor, and Carpenter does not disagree. The PFD’s cost

analysis does not engage the record beyond listing the highly variable cost estimates and the

intervenors’ concerns about those estimates across all proposed routes.41 Despite this recognized

uncertainty and variability, the PFD describes Route 894, which costs an estimated $1.681

billion, as “performing favorably.”42

       The PFD identifies only one comparative advantage for Route 894—that it costs only

2.7% more than the cheapest proposed route (one not considered a Focus Route).43 The PFD’s

reasoning after this comparison is misleading and inaccurate. The PFD compares 894 to the

cheapest route and yet only compares Routes 392 and 296 to 894, rather than using the same

metric.44 As a result, it fails to note that Route 296 is only approximately 2.9% more than the

cheapest route. Not only does this minor statistical difference show that all the focus routes fall

        While the PFD’s ultimate routing recommendation indicates that it did not find cost to be

a distinguishing factor, Carpenter excepts to the characterization that Route 894 “performs

favorably on cost” and FOF 163-164 to the extent that they support Route 894.

                       vi. Engineering Constraints

        Carpenter also excepts to Findings of Fact 181-183 and Conclusion of Law 16 to the

extent that they support Route 894. Link J31 is the optimal crossing location for the Colorado

River        because     it    parallels     an     existing      compatible        pipeline   corridor,   which

consolidates environmental disturbance and reduces fragmentation of the surrounding area.45

Additionally, compared with other crossings, Segment J31 is farther from Colorado Bend State

Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park, whereas alternative crossings like Link J22 sit within half a

mile of these parks.

                       vii. Paralleling

        Carpenter also excepts to Findings of Fact 177-180 and Conclusion of Law 16 to the

extent that it supports Route 894.

        Route 894’s Link J22 would irreparably affect Carpenter Land and Cattle Co.’s

Greenwood Creek Ranch and the Colorado River on which it sits, to an unacceptable extent. The

Greenwood Creek Ranch has a rich and storied history and is a destination location for hundreds

of people each year who come to stay there.46 Link J22 has a turning structure on the ranch’s

property that then causes the link to run directly between the guest cabin and Greenwood Creek

and is within the 500-foot notice corridor of that guest house and brings the line even closer to

the main lodge.47 Link J22 also goes directly through (and by necessity over) the highest point on

the property, which is the “Lookout,” and would forever change the interrupted views from this

vista. The Lookout makes up the entirety of what the Applicants have marked as Tract 1637. It

has been part of Greenwood since the 1940s. Routing over this lookout peak will increase the

already atrocious visual impacts of the proposed line from both State Parks and from the

remainder of Greenwood and their neighbors.48

       The Application has very limited instances with links that follow existing transmission

lines or other compatible rights-of-way, or property lines, rather than further fragmenting habitat

and properties. This approach is contrary to the commonly held value in this state of preserving

large parcels of land to promote land stewardship.49 As a result, the Commission should not

approve Route 894, which is an abject departure from any routing criteria.

                        viii. Prudent Avoidance

       The PFD expresses prudent avoidance concerns regarding Route 296 specifically

regarding its proximity to the Florence ISD school. However, this concern can be easily

mitigated by the Joint Applicants, and as a result, prudent avoidance should not be used as a

basis to exclude Route 296. And in the event that the Commissioners determine that Route 296

is unacceptable due to this proximity to the school even with this adjustment, the Commissioners

should then choose Route 572 which follows the same links as Route 894 through Bell and

Williamson Counties.

       As acknowledged in the PFD,50 the Commission defines prudent avoidance as “[t]he

limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable

investments of money and effort.”51 The PFD further acknowledges that “[p]rudent avoidance

does not mean that a proposed transmission line must avoid habitable structures at all costs, but

that reasonable alternatives must be considered.”52 However, in the end, the PFD sole routing

recommendation boils down to a counting of habitable structures within the Commission’s notice

corridor of 500 feet (actually 520 feet as used in the Application).53 When giving their routing

recommendation, the PFD then explicitly states that “Route 894 performs favorably on habitable

structures,”54 rather than using the term “prudent avoidance.” In the three sentences explaining

the thought process on prudent avoidance, the PFD appears to conflate “habitable structures” and

“prudent avoidance” as like-for-like, when Commission rules and precedent require a much more

comprehensive approach. As the Applicants state unequivocally, all routes comply with the

policy of prudent avoidance.

       Carpenter urges that a simple count of habitable structures does not constitute a

determination of prudent avoidance, nor is it even a factor that the legislature has required the

Commission to weigh in evaluating a CCN application.55 Encountering habitable structures must

be balanced against the preference for routing along roadways and property lines, for example,

rather than bisecting undisturbed properties.56 Such counting within the applicable notice

distance from the proposed transmission line routing alternative is not a substitute for an

examination of moderating impacts on the community or affected landowners, or for prudent

avoidance,57 and runs directly counter to the mandate the legislature has given the Commission.58

When analyzed comprehensively, Route 894 is not preferable to Route 296 or Route 572.

       Greenwood Creek Ranch provides an instructive example of the arbitrary nature of 500

feet as a measure of habitable structure impacts.               There are multiple habitable structures on

Greenwood Creek Ranch that would be severely impacted if Route 894 were approved.59 Link

J22 takes a sharp angle and splits between two habitable structures on the property. First, is the

guest house that is noted in the Application as a habitable structure within 500 feet of the

proposed Link J22.60 Link J22 is on the property where the guest house is located.61 Second, is

the Main Lodge which serves as a gathering place all year round for hundreds of guests, friends,

and family.62 Although outside the 520 foot notice corridor, it is less than 600 feet from the

apparent centerline of Link J22, it is nonetheless a significant source of exposure to the people

that gather at Greenwood, and highly disruptive of the focus on nature experience at the lodge. 63

The 500 foot metric is simply a notice corridor; it is not determinative of impacts to habitable

structures or the people who use them.64

       Extensive Commission precedent supports a determination that, after following the

mandate to analyze all criteria, prudent avoidance was satisfied even if a route had more

structures estimated within the notice corridor than other routes.65 In this specific case, focusing

solely on the number of habitable structures runs counter to the mandate to conduct the required

and Commission Staff70 agree that Routes 296 and 572 meet the Legislature’s and Commission’s

prudent avoidance requirements. Routes 296 and 572 also specifically avoid Links E6 and E12,

which numerous intervenors have taken issue with.71 And when taking that criteria into account,

especially considering Route 894’s potential impact on the Lampasas, Colorado, and San Saba

Rivers,72 along with other parties’ own unique and numerous habitable structure issues that are

imposed upon it by Route 894,73 Routes 296 and 572 more strictly adhere to the mandate of

prudent avoidance.

distance from this school, well beyond 500 feet, and it is vital for the Commission to recognize

that it has approved siting of projects near schools extremely recently.74 If there is an individual

add distance between the line and that structure,75 with subject matter expert Dr. Marcus

Turnbough testifying that “there’s always an opportunity to mitigate the potential impact of an

alignment by a minor adjustment.”76 Alternatively, Route 572 does not include Link F34 and is

available to the Commission as a reasonable balancing of all factors in this proceeding, while

also offering many of the same benefits as Route 296 compared to Route 894.

        The Commission must analyze prudent avoidance comprehensively, as prior Commission

practice and the complexity of the issue demand, rather than reduce it to a crude counting

exercise of habitable structures. When viewed in this way, both Routes 296 and 572 meet the

statutory requirements on prudent avoidance, and thus it should not be used as a way to

disqualify either route, especially when they both compare so favorably against Route 894 in

other equally important respects.

                                     IV.    CONCLUSION

        For these reasons, Carpenter respectfully requests that if the Commission rejects the PFD

on the issue of need, that it also reject the routing recommendation in the PFD and instead select

Route 296 adjusted as discussed in these Exceptions, Route 572, or a hybrid of Route 572 and

296 that avoids Link F34 in its entirety as previously discussed in Carpenter’s Reply Brief.77

        Carpenter Land and Cattle Co. (Carpenter) files these Limited Exceptions (Exceptions) to

 the alternative recommendation of route selection offered in the Proposal for Decision (PFD).

 Pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies Memorandum, filed August 20, 2026, these Limited

 Exceptions are timely filed on or before September 2,2026. Carpenter does not except to the

 primary recommendation in the Proposal for Decision.


                                      I.    INTRODUCTION

        The Carpenter family raises these limited exceptions focused solely on       the PFD's

 alternative routing recommendation of Route 894.       The Carpenters have owned Greenwood

 Creek Ranch on the east side of the Colorado River for generations.1 This is the point at which

 Route 894 would cross the Colorado River just south of the Colorado Bend State Park and the

 recently acquired Post Oak Ridge State Park.2 The Carpenter family excepts to this routing

 recommendation because it will have permanent and scarring impacts on the Colorado River and

                       viii. Prudent Avoidance

       The PFD expresses prudent avoidance concerns regarding Route 296 specifically

regarding its proximity to the Florence ISD school. However, this concern can be easily

mitigated by the Joint Applicants, and as a result, prudent avoidance should not be used as a

basis to exclude Route 296. And in the event that the Commissioners determine that Route 296

is unacceptable due to this proximity to the school even with this adjustment, the Commissioners

should then choose Route 572 which follows the same links as Route 894 through Bell and

Williamson Counties.
